coredata.dc:description: BaCeO3 is a mixed oxide with a wide variety of potential applications, from solid-oxide fuel cells to hydrogen detectors. However, a common issue in its preparation is the preferential formation of carbonates. This poses an issue when the material is intended for use in bulk REBCO growth, a role it otherwise appears suitable for. In this work, we present a synthesis of BaCeO3 through the carbonate-free co-precipitation method based on the acid-base and redox behaviors of its constituent cations, with carbon-containing precursors and precipitating agents purposefully omitted. Three pH-adjusting/precipitation agents were compared together with the comparison of cerium(III) nitrate and cerium dioxide as the sources of cerium cations. Through this, the elimination of carbonate content (confirmed by XRD but also with more carbonate-sensitive Raman spectroscopy) as well as significant reduction in average particle size was achieved. The obtained powder is therefore suitable for the growth of bulk REBCO crystals.

head.ce:title: Co-precipitation synthesis of carbon-free BaCeO3 for use in bulk superconductor growth

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: BaCeO3 is a mixed oxide with a wide variety of potential applications, from solid-oxide fuel cells to hydrogen detectors. However, a common issue in its preparation is the preferential formation of carbonates. This poses an issue when the material is intended for use in bulk REBCO growth, a role it otherwise appears suitable for. In this work, we present a synthesis of BaCeO3 through the carbonate-free co-precipitation method based on the acid-base and redox behaviors of its constituent cations, with carbon-containing precursors and precipitating agents purposefully omitted. Three pH-adjusting/precipitation agents were compared together with the comparison of cerium(III) nitrate and cerium dioxide as the sources of cerium cations. Through this, the elimination of carbonate content (confirmed by XRD but also with more carbonate-sensitive Raman spectroscopy) as well as significant reduction in average particle size was achieved. The obtained powder is therefore suitable for the growth of bulk REBCO crystals.

ce:section.ce:para: Barium cerate (BaCeO3) is a prospective material in the field of electrochemistry, of interest mainly due to its mixed proton and electron conduction properties. This makes it a candidate for the construction of ceramic membranes intended for solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) as well as offering potential applications as electrode materials or catalytic membranes [1–3]. This property is commonplace among perovskite mixed oxides (oxides with multiple elements as cations) with the general ABO3 formula; however, BaCeO3-derived perovskites exhibit the strongest proton conductivity of these materials in combination with improving oxygen ionic conduction as the temperature rises [4]. However, another, less explored vector for the use of BaCeO3 is as an additive to REBCO superconductors (RE-Ba-Cu-O system, RE = Y, Gd, Eu, Sm…), where it can assist in pinning magnetic flux lines and improving the material’s performance [5]. At the same time, the mixed oxide has demonstrated similar impacts on the growth of non-superconducting Y211 phase as CeO2, controlled growth of which can be used to induce flux pinning as well. Unlike CeO2, however, using BaCeO3 for this purpose does not lead to the undesired formation of copper(II) oxide during the growth process [6].

Despite the relative simplicity of the BaO-CeO2 pseudobinary diagram [7], which only contains one stoichiometric phase – the aforementioned BaCeO3 – this phase has a number of crystal modifications depending on the temperature. Two low-temperature orthorhombic Pmcn and Imcn modifications are stable below approximately 290 °C and 400 °C respectively; at around 400 °C the orthorhombic structure transforms into a rhombohedral one (R–3c). Above 900 °C, a cubic modification (Pm–3 m) is stabilized [7–10].

A variety of methods have been explored to prepare BaCeO3 powders, which can be broadly classified into two categories. The first is a solid-state reaction, which involves preparing a stoichiometric mixture of precursor oxides or carbonates, most commonly CeO2 and either BaCO3 or BaO2, that are then calcined [11,12]. This process is technologically simple, but presents issues regarding homogeneity, as well as producing relatively large particle size in the resulting powder that can negatively affect the dispersion of the powder when preparing the mix for YBCO growth. The second category – “wet” methods – is based on synthesis from solutions of the required metal cations and therefore achieves a significantly improved homogeneity while offering the potential for much lower overall particle size, depending on synthesis conditions. Widely used among these is co-precipitation, which is based on mixing a precipitating agent with a solution containing cations, resulting in the formation of a fine precipitate which is usually a mixture of hydroxides (or other hydrated forms) containing both cations. This fine powder mixture is highly reactive; on the other hand, the stoichiometry of the precipitate must be controlled [13]. Nevertheless, when co-precipitation is optimized, the precursor powder forms mixed oxides at a lower temperature than usually required. Moreover, the certainty of high cation homogeneity required for example in optical applications is easier to achieve [14]. With BaCeO3, this is usually done by using oxalates or carbonates as the precipitating agent [15,16].

A common issue in both types of preparation is the formation of BaCO3, caused by a high affinity of barium(II) ions towards CO2, which is further exacerbated by the use of carbon-based precipitating agents. Thermal decomposition of barium carbonate demands longer calcination times and higher temperatures, which runs counter to the particle size requirements [17]. The presence of carbon in the mixture is detrimental to the formation of the Y123 superconducting phase [18], however, alternative methods such as combustion synthesis are difficult to control and can produce toxic gases during the reaction [19]. Typically, ammonium carbonates are used to achieve high pH values, but the easy formation of BaCO3 precludes their use, and alternatives must be found. In this work, we present a method for the preparation of carbon-free BaCeO3 powders, based on co-precipitation of cerium and barium using a combination of their acid-base and redox properties.

BaCeO3 was prepared by co-precipitation of metal cations from an aqueous solution by means of a pH change with simultaneous oxidation of cerium, forming insoluble CeO2. Solutions of the constituent cations were prepared separately; prior to the synthesis, distilled water used for dissolving was boiled to minimize the presence of CO2 and thus reduce the potential for the formation of BaCO3. Ba(OH)2·8H2O was used as a barium source, dissolved in diluted nitric acid, with CeO2 or Ce(NO3)3 used as cerium sources. CeO2 was dissolved by similar means as Ba(OH)2·8H2O, with simultaneous reduction by hydrogen peroxide, while dissolution of Ce(NO3)3·6 H2O in water does not require acidification. Ammonia, tetramethylammonium hydroxide (TMAH) or sodium hydroxide were used as precipitating agents. The entire process was further optimized to minimize exposure of the samples to carbon contamination and with the aim to minimize the particle size of the obtained BaCeO3.

For the synthesis, the following chemicals were used: HNO3 (65%, Lachner, p.a.), H2O2 (30%, Lachner, p.a.), NaOH (Lachner, >99.7%), NH3 (25%, Lachner, p.a.) and N(CH3)4OH ·5H2O (Sigma-Aldrich, >97%). Ba(OH)2·8H2O (Fluka Analytical, >98%) was used as the barium source. Two separate sources of cerium were used: CeO2 (Sigma-Aldrich, >99%) and Ce(NO3)3·6H2O (Sigma-Aldrich, >99%).

Ba(OH)2·8H2O was dissolved in a minimal amount of distilled water by heating at 80 °C and adding HNO3 dropwise under constant stirring until all hydroxide was dissolved. In all preparations, Ba(OH)2·8H2O was always used in a 20 wt.% surplus to the stoichiometric amount necessary for the formation of BaCeO3. This surplus is required due to the difficulty of quantitatively precipitating barium compounds other than carbonates using pH change. The dissolution of barium hydroxide proceeds according to the equation (Eq. (1)):
(1) Ba(OH)2 + 2 HNO3→Ba(NO3)2 + H2O

Cerium(III) nitrate was directly dissolved in hot (80 °C) water. Dissolving CeO2 required adding a surplus of HNO3 and H2O2 dropwise for the reduction of tetravalent cerium to its soluble trivalent form, in accordance with equation (Eq. (2)):
(2) 2 CeO2+6 HNO3 + H2O2→2 Ce(NO3)3 + 4 H2O + O2

The resulting solutions of Ba and Ce ions were then mixed and left to cool under stirring. Precipitation of the powder precursor was performed using a mixture of H2O2 and a pH-controlling precipitating agent. In the case of samples designated BCO_1 and BCO_2, 15 ml NH3 and a combination of 15 ml NH3 and 5 ml TMAH were used respectively, with 15 ml NaOH saturated solution being used in samples designated BCO_3 and BCO_4 (as can be seen in Table 1 ). After the initial precipitation, pH was further adjusted with the respective precipitating agent until it reached a maximum of pH = 10 for NH3, pH = 12.5 for TMAH and pH = 13.5 for NaOH. Additional H2O2 was dropped at the same time to ensure complete oxidation and precipitation. The resulting suspension was immediately placed under argon atmosphere (to prevent absorption of CO2 from the air) and allowed some time to facilitate the decomposition of H2O2. The precipitation proceeds according to the following for NaOH, with analogous equations for other precipitating agents (Eq. (3) and 4):
(3) 2 Ce(NO3)3 + 3 NaOH + 2 H2O2 → + 2CeO2 + 3 NaNO3 + 4 H2O
(4) Ba(NO3)2 + 2 NaOH → 2 Na(NO3)2 + Ba(OH)2 + H2O

The suspension was further decanted thrice (five times in samples designated BCO_4) with distilled water and filtered with pressure assistance, with the filtration cake washed through with NH3 and water. The acquired solid phase was then dried in vacuum at 115 °C overnight and annealed in air at 800 °C or 1000 °C for one hour depending on the sample (as can be seen in Table 1). At the end of the annealing process, the powder was quenched to room temperature in order to minimize time spent above the formation temperature of BaCO3 (Fig. 1 ).

X-ray powder diffraction data was obtained using a Bruker D2 Phaser diffractometer with Bragg-Brentano parafocusing geometry using CoKα radiation (λ = 1.79021 Å, U = 34 kV, I = 20 mA). Data evaluation including Rietveld refinement was performed in the X’Pert HighScore Plus software package using the PDF4+ database.

Raman spectra were measured on a Thermo-Scientific model DXR Microscope Raman dispersion spectrometer equipped with an Olympus confocal microscope. The excitation source used was a Nd:YAG laser at 532 nm wavelength and an input power of 9 mW. A 900 hole/mm lattice was used. Detection was performed using a cooled CCD camera. For all samples, a magnification of 50x was applied, with samples measured through a 50 µm pinhole aperture at ten accumulations per spectrum. Each spectrum was measured thrice and then averaged.

Simultaneous thermal analysis (STA) with attached mass spectrometry (MS) was performed on a Setatram Setsys Evolution TG-DTA machine under air and in the temperature range of 25–1400 °C, measuring both heat flow and mass reduction. Further analysis of the formed gases was performed using a connected Pfeiffer Vacuum OmniStarTM quadrupole mass spectrometer.

Particle size was analyzed using laser diffraction (LD) with an ultrasonic probe applied prior to measurement. The samples were then imaged using an EFTEM Jeol 2200 FS transmission electron microscope capable of accelerating voltage of 200 kV and equipped with an EDS probe. The morphology and size of particles was observed.

The three initial samples (BCO_1, BCO_2 and BCO_3) were compared to understand the effects of using different pH controlling agents – ammonia, TMAH and NaOH – on the precipitation process. For samples designated BCO_2 and BCO_3, the process was modified using Ce(NO3)3 as a source of Ce instead of CeO2, the dissolution of which has proven to be highly time consuming.

As can be seen in Fig. 2 , the XRD measurements of precipitated mixtures after annealing showed significant difference between the samples. The most intense peaks for both BaCeO3 and CeO2 lie at a nearly identical position (around 33.5 °2θ and 33.2 °2θ respectively); however, the remaining peaks provide an acceptable substitute for the purposes of determining the presence of other phases. Of further notice are the two peaks characteristic for BaCO3 in the 27.5–28.5 °2θ, which can serve as an indicator of its presence.

Of the three above-mentioned samples, all showed significant content of CeO2, with sample BCO_1 containing only CeO2, without any barium-containing phases detected regardless of the annealing temperature. This indicated that the pH was not high enough to precipitate the barium(II) cations in sufficient quantity, and a stronger base must be used. In the sample BCO_2, BaCeO3 was clearly formed, although it remained a minority phase. Its content – as calculated by the Rietveld method – was approx. 13.2% and 13.9% after annealing at 800 °C or 1000 °C respectively, with the remainder (86.8% and 86.1% respectively) made up by CeO2. Notably, the amount of BaCeO3 was similar in both samples, regardless of the annealing temperature, suggesting that the formation of further oxide remained limited by the lack of Ba precipitation rather than the annealing process. The third sample (BCO_3) showed a steep rise in the intensity of peaks belonging to the BaCeO3 phase, thus confirming it as the majority phase. The use of NaOH as precipitating agent therefore led to a significant improvement in terms of the Ba precipitation; however, a degree of contamination can also be observed in the sample. Some weak reflections (most notable between 35 and 45 °2θ) were present at both annealing temperatures and were most likely the result of nitrate formation. Though low in intensity, these peaks block out positions of reflections necessary to perform Rietveld refinement and obtain CeO2 content for this sample. However, a weak signal can still be found in the position of the second strongest peak characteristic for CeO2 (at 55.5 °2θ), suggesting it is indeed present.

To confirm the phase composition of samples BCO_1 and BCO_2, Raman spectroscopy was performed on samples after annealing at both temperatures (Fig. 3 ). All of the spectra are dominated by the symmetric T2g Ce-O vibration at 465 cm-1 [22]; its high intensity is due to high symmetry in CeO2 and is not indicative of high ceria content. Of more interest is the 50–400 cm-1 region where signals of BaCeO3 are found [23] and the 1060 cm-1 signal which corresponds to the presence of BaCO3 [24]. The Raman spectra for sample BCO_3 has been omitted, as the presence of contaminants (probably nitrates) is already clear from the XRD.

These Raman spectra confirmed the findings from the XRD analysis. In both BCO_1 and BCO_2 samples, the intensive signal at 1060 cm-1 characteristic for BaCO3 was absent regardless of annealing temperature. Contrary to the XRD detection limit, the Raman spectroscopy could reveal even the traces of BaCO3. In samples BCO_1, the desired BaCeO3 phase was absent as was obtained by XRD analysis. The same was not true for the BCO_2 sample, the spectra of which showed the presence of BaCeO3 in samples annealed both at 800 and 1000 °C.

To further establish the contamination from the precipitation process, a STA/TG/MS measurement of the precipitated precursor powder after drying but prior to annealing was performed, with its results in Fig. 4 . Of special interest was the determination of the temperatures at which gases resulting from decomposition of undesirable nitrates and carbonates escape the sample. When contrasted against net weight loss in the same range, this provides insight into the amount of each contaminant, as well as enabling matching the decomposition temperatures to the presence of various contaminants.

This analysis explained why both carbonate and nitrate contaminants were present in the BCO_3 sample. Below 250 °C, a significant quantity of adsorbed water was evaporated, which does not affect the sample – however, between 700 °C and 1000 °C, a significant amount of NOx gases was released, corresponding with an 8% weight decrease in the sample. This suggests a high level of nitrate contamination. Furthermore, a spike in CO2 release can be observed above 1000 °C. This suggests the carbonates in the sample do not begin to decompose before this temperature is reached. The amount of CO2 released peaks above 1300 °C, which is consistent with the decomposition of BaCO3 [17]; this process corresponds to a mass loss of nearly 2.5 wt.%. The total content of contaminants (CO2 and NOx) was determined to be close to 12 wt.% by the analysis.

Based on these findings, a fourth sample (BCO_4) was prepared. In this sample, an effort was made to minimize the amount of nitrogen content by replacing Ce(NO3)3 with CeO2 as a source of cerium, as well as increasing the number of purification cycles of decantation and washing of the filtration cake to ensure that all undesirable material is removed from the product. The resulting powder was then analyzed prior to annealing by the STA/TG/MS method to confirm that any contaminants would be eliminated during heat treatment.

As can be seen in Fig. 5 , a significantly lower total amount of contaminants was present in the BCO_4 sample compared to BCO_3. After water evaporation observed at lower temperatures, the net mass loss of the sample after reaching 600 °C amounted only to roughly 3 wt.%. While a spike in the amount of released NO and NO2 was observed in the temperature range of 600 °C to 900 °C, this did not correspond with a significant decrease in mass (approx. <1%) and the nitrate contamination is therefore likely minimal. Similarly, escaping CO2 was observed in the 700 °C to 1000 °C range, but only accounts for about 2% mass loss, indicating the carbonate content was likewise minimal. A much less intensive CO2 emission was observed above 1360 °C, which corresponds to the decomposition of BaCO3, however no measurable mass loss was observed in the in the sample above 1100 °C. It is therefore likely that this is not connected to any carbonate content in the sample itself.

The lack of detectable BaCO3 in the powder annealed at 1000 °C is presumably the result of measures taken to eliminate CO2 from the starting solutions through eliminating carbon-containing precursors and boiling the distilled water used in the process, which significantly reduced the amount of carbonate that formed during precipitation. The remaining carbonate is then formed as a considerably more reactive powder, as is typical for coprecipitation. This allows the carbonate to be eliminated during the annealing process without reaching its regular decomposition temperature, as visible in Fig. 5. Quenching the powder rapidly instead of allowing it to cool slowly then prevents exposition to atmospheric CO2 at elevated temperatures, preventing formation of BaCO3 at the end of the process.

In samples observed using TEM, a common trend is the increase in overall particle size in samples annealed at 1000 °C compared to samples annealed at 800 °C. The effect of precipitation agents on the particle size is difficult to quantify, although it appears that the lower bound of particle sizes was higher in samples where NaOH was used as the precipitation agent compared to the rest of the series.

Since XRD analysis indicated that the samples with high BaCeO3 content were not single-phase, EDS analysis was used to distinguish between CeO2 and BaCeO3 particles. In all the samples observed, a systematic size disparity was observed, with CeO2 particles exhibiting a much lower overall size than BaCeO3 particles. This difference is most visible in Fig. 11, which shows that the smallest particles do not contain barium at either annealing temperature. Particles containing only barium were not observed by this method, confirming the presence of BaCeO3 and CeO2 only.

Of special note is imaging of BaCeO3 particles from sample BAO_4 annealed at 1000 °C. Although the average size of these particles apparently lies well above 500 nm, a degree of peak widening can be observed in the XRD analysis (Fig. 6). One possible explanation arises from the TEM imaging (Fig. 12 ), which shows lines of increased material density present in the individual particles. These lines are commonly indicative of residual material stress resulting from rapid cooling [25]. This demonstrates the necessity of using complementary analysis methods in crystallite size determination.

A carbonate-free co-precipitation procedure for the preparation of BaCeO3 was developed. The precipitation was achieved by combining acid-base and redox behavior of cerium and barium cations. NH3, TMAH and NaOH were compared as agents setting high pH values. Annealing temperatures of 800 °C and 1000 °C were used to crystallize the powders. Due to the nature of the barium and cerium ions, a dual approach to precipitation was chosen, utilizing simultaneous pH adjustment to precipitate barium(II) ions and H2O2 to oxidize cerium into a cerium(IV) state, forming highly insoluble CeO2.

In general, several mixtures of BaCeO3 and CeO2 with minimal carbonate contamination were obtained. BaCeO3 with minor CeO2 presence was prepared when NaOH was used for the pH adjustment of the solution containing barium hydroxide and cerium(III) nitrate, while the usage of TMAH provided only minor BaCeO3 content. However, the samples precipitated by NaOH were contaminated by nitrates, which were difficult to eliminate by decantation. This was solved by replacement of the cerium source (CeO2 instead of Ce(NO3)3), with the resulting mixture made up of majority BaCeO3 phase and minority CeO2. While in some samples, BaCO3 presence was detected, this was not the case for the optimized sample annealed at 1000 °C, which was carbonate-free.

Crystallite size as observed by TEM was in the order of magnitude of hundreds of nanometers for BaCeO3 particles. When CeO2 was present as a secondary phase, its particle size was systematically smaller than that of BaCeO3.

As CeO2 is a commonly used additive for the successful growth of YBCO single-domain crystals using the top-seeded melt-growth method, its presence in the prepared carbonate-free samples does not pose an obstacle for use in such a growth.
